Tambora is identified as a major volcanic forcing behind the anomalous 1816 Northern Hemisphere climate, while local atmospheric variability also mattered.
The study infers species-specific responses from fisheries records, air temperatures and phenological knowledge. Direct fish behavior and mortality were not measured in 1816.
Weak alewife availability interacted with crop failure and food demand, shifting fishing effort toward marine species including mackerel.
The emergency shift in fishing effort persisted after the immediate climate anomaly, creating a path-dependent structural adaptation.
Tambora forcing contributed to the exceptionally cold 1816 summer in the Czech Lands; background climate and circulation variability also influenced conditions.
Persistent wet conditions damaged cereals and yields, contributing to shortage and later grain-price pressure.
Cold and damaging 1816 weather contributed to poor grain harvests followed by widespread price increases in 1817.
The Geneva cold summer occurred in the post-Tambora climate anomaly, with regional circulation and cloudiness shaping the local expression.

The cold, rainy Geneva summer helped keep the literary group indoors and formed the documented setting for the ghost-story challenge from which Frankenstein emerged. This is a contributing cultural context, not a claim that climate alone caused the work.
Post-eruption cold conditions contributed to unusual Alpine snow conditions during 1816–1817.
Snow storage increased the water available for melt, but modeling indicates spring 1817 snowfall and intense triggering rainfall were more immediate drivers than surviving 1816 snow alone.
Multiple proxy lines attribute a significant part of the southern China 1816 cold excursion to Tambora-era volcanic forcing.

Cold conditions and reconstructed drying tendencies occurred together, but proxy systems disagree spatially, so the hydroclimate connection is stored as associated rather than simple deterministic causation.
These are distinct state-formation/diplomatic processes in different regions. The link is chronological only and exists to support comparative political timelines, not causation.
Both occurred in southern Africa in 1816 but arose from different political systems. This relationship is explicitly non-causal and useful for regional comparison.
Local tephra deposition damaged croplands directly; this differs from remote aerosol climate effects.
Loss of food production contributed to starvation in the local aftermath.
Rice relief and distress sales are documented responses to famine. This edge reads response → crisis; it does not establish relief effectiveness.
Review combines drying proxies with simulations of weakened monsoon circulation following volcanic forcing.
Punitive orders enabled the expedition; Wallis’s conduct exceeded instructions to spare women and children.
The massacre preceded the proclamation within the same colonial campaign; chronology does not prove that the massacre caused the policy.
Organization and training provided capacity for the later campaign; this is a curated interpretation of the chronology.
Crossing placed the army in Chile before Chacabuco; the chronology alone does not establish why the battle was won.
Price pressure preceded the stock survey; the survey’s specific trigger was a provincial request.
Public imports addressed scarcity; beneficial price effects remain contested.
Reduced-price sales targeted food access after price escalation.
Modeled production losses alone do not explain the regional malnutrition gradient.
The same reconstructed weather produced differing modeled crop responses.
Simulations attribute a substantial increase in cold-event likelihood to volcanic forcing.
Cold and wet anomalies co-occurred; their attribution strengths differ.

Jefferson describes drought and frost as crop pressures; the resulting harvest figure remains his forecast.
Author argues sufficient growing-season water helped rice; rainfall cannot be isolated from varieties, institutions and local conditions.
Recovery follows an existing crisis; no Tambora→1814 edge.
Administrative harvest classifications show continuing recovery; no universal volcanic crop-failure sequence is established.
Cholera fear and flight observed; no quantified transmission claim.
Two epidemic records; direction of transmission not proven by ordering.
Synthesis supports prolonged crisis; not all mortality attributable to starvation or volcano alone.
Subsequent epidemic, with no disease identification or proven nutritional cause.
Context and later response; multifactorial disease causation remains uncertain.

Inferred contribution: arrival made foreign artists available for proposed recruitment. The sources do not establish that arrival caused policy planning; instruction and disbursement require separate records.
Punitive orders precede the diary’s transfer of captive children; individual capture circumstances are not established.
A later official account conflicts with Wallis’s attack narrative as assessed by the museum. Documentation is not corroboration of the resistance claim.
Contemporaneous diary reports connect heavy rain, flooding and threatened crops; losses are forecasts, not audited totals.
Two independent May records illustrate shipping used for diplomacy and food exchange; neither shipment caused the other.
